The provision for loan losses on acquired loans was unchanged for 2013 from 2012 at $7 million.  Net charge-offs decreased to nine basis points of average acquired loans for 2013 from 12 basis points of average acquired loans for 2012.  For the years ended 2013 and 2012, we recognized provision for credit losses related to our unfunded loan commitments of $2 million and $1 million, respectively.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Period end balances in our commercial loan portfolio grew $1.0 billion, or 8%, to $13.1 billion and our indirect auto loan portfolio more than doubled in 2013 to $1.5 billion at December 31, 2013 from $601 million at December 31, 2012.  The decrease in our residential real estate loans reflected industry wide prepayment levels.  </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">The $828 million decrease in our available for sale and held to maturity investment securities portfolio reflected the balance sheet rotation strategy we executed during 2013 whereby we used cash flows received on our residential mortgage-backed investment securities portfolio and investment security sales to fund loan growth. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Transactional deposit balances increased $515 million, reflecting our continued efforts to grow our customer base, reposition our account mix, and increase our lower cost deposits.  Short-term borrowings increased $1.8 billion from December 31, 2012 as we used short-term borrowings to fund asset growth due to the planned run off of our money market deposit accounts and certificates of deposit.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">The increase in our noninterest income for 2013 from 2012 was driven by increases in deposit service charges, merchant and card fees, and wealth management services, which reflect the full year impact of our HSBC Branch Acquisition.  These increases were offset by decreases in mortgage banking revenues and capital markets income.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Total GAAP noninterest expenses were $931 million for 2013, down approximately $120 million from 2012.  Excluding merger and acquisition integration expenses and restructuring charges in 2012, our noninterest expenses increased $64 million.</font></div><a name="s3C7DB94819625486A661C29A1466D925"></a><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:bold;">CRITICAL ACCOUNTING POLICIES AND ESTIMATES</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">We evaluate those accounting policies and estimates that we judge to be critical: those most important to the presentation of our financial condition and results of operations, and those which require our most subjective and complex judgments. Accordingly, our accounting estimates relating to the valuation of our investment securities, prepayment assumptions on our collateralized mortgage obligations and mortgage-backed securities, adequacy of our allowance for loan losses, the accounting treatment and valuation of our acquired loans, and the analysis of the carrying value of goodwill for impairment are deemed to be critical as our judgments could have a material effect on our results of operations. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:bold;">Investment Securities</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">As of </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;text-decoration:none;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, our available for sale and held to maturity investment securities totaled </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;text-decoration:none;">$11.9 billion</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, or </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;text-decoration:none;">31%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;of our total assets. We use third party pricing services to value our investment securities portfolio, which is comprised almost entirely of Level 2 fair value measured securities. Fair value of our investment securities is based upon quoted market prices of identical securities, where available. If such quoted prices are not available, fair </font></div><br><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:9pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">50</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><br><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">value is determined using valuation models that consider cash flow, security structure, and other observable information. For the vast majority of the portfolio, we validate the prices received from these third parties, on a monthly basis, by comparing them to prices provided by a different independent pricing service. For the remaining securities that are priced by these third parties where we are unable to obtain a secondary independent price, we review material price changes for reasonableness based upon changes in interest rates, credit outlook based upon spreads for similar securities, and the weighted average life of the debt securities. We have also reviewed detailed valuation methodologies provided to us by our pricing services. We did not adjust any of the prices provided to us by the independent pricing services at </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;text-decoration:none;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;or </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;text-decoration:none;">2013</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">. Where sufficient information is not available from the pricing services to produce a reliable valuation, we estimate fair value based on broker quotes, which are reviewed using the same process that is applied to our securities priced by pricing services where we are unable to obtain a secondary independent price, or based on internally developed models which consider estimated prepayment speeds, losses, recoveries, default rates that are implied by the underlying performance of collateral in the structure or similar structures, and discount rates that are implied by market prices for similar securities and collateral structure types.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Our investment securities portfolio includes residential mortgage backed securities and collateralized mortgage obligations. As the underlying collateral of each of these securities is comprised of a large number of similar residential mortgage loans for which prepayments are probable and the timing and amount of such prepayments can be reasonably estimated, we estimate future principal prepayments of the underlying residential mortgage loans to determine a constant effective yield used to apply the interest method, with retroactive adjustments as warranted.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">In order to compute the constant effective yield for these securities, we estimate pooled level cash flows for each security based on a variety of factors, including historical and projected prepayment speeds, current and future interest rates, yield curve assumptions, security issuer and the current political environment.  These cash flows are then translated into security level cash flows based on the tranche we own and the unique structure and status of each security.  At </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;text-decoration:none;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, the par value of our portfolio of residential mortgage-backed securities totaled </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;text-decoration:none;">$7.1 billion</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, which included </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;text-decoration:none;">$6.6 billion</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;of collateralized mortgage obligations.  In the determination of our constant effective yield, we estimate that we will receive </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;text-decoration:none;">$1.3 billion</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;of principal cash flows on our collateralized mortgage obligations over the next 12 months.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:bold;">Allowance for Loan Losses</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">We establish our allowance for loan losses through a provision for credit losses.  The level of the allowance for loan losses is based on our evaluation of the overall credit quality of our total loan portfolio. We segregate our loans between loans we originated which are accounted for under the amortized cost method (referred to as &#8220;originated&#8221; loans) and loans acquired (referred to as &#8220;acquired&#8221; loans), as acquired loans were originally recorded at fair value, which included an estimate of lifetime credit losses, resulting in no carryover of the related allowance for loan losses.   We continue to monitor and modify the level of our allowance for loan losses to ensure it is adequate to cover losses inherent in our loan portfolio. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;text-decoration:underline;">Originated loans</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">We determine our allowance for loan losses by portfolio segment, which consists of commercial loans and consumer loans. Our commercial loan portfolio includes both business and commercial real estate loans. Our consumer loan portfolio includes residential real estate, home equity, indirect auto, credit card and other consumer loans.  The allowance for loan losses is comprised of two components.  The first component covers pools of loans for which there are incurred losses that are not yet individually identifiable.  The allowance for pools of loans is based on net historical loan loss experience for similar loans with similar inherent risk characteristics and performance trends adjusted, as appropriate, for quantitative and qualitative risk factors specific to respective loan types.  The second component covers loans that have been identified as impaired or are nonperforming as well as troubled debt restructurings (&#8220;TDRs&#8221;.) </font></div><br><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:9pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">51</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><br><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;">Commercial loan portfolio</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Commercial loans are initially evaluated using quantitative models whereby loans are grouped into pools based on similar risk characteristics such as loan type and grade to determine the historical loss rate.  Our loan grading system is described in &#8220;Management&#8217;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations&#8221; under the heading &#8220;Credit Risk.&#8221; By loan type, the historical loss experience over an established loss emergence and look back period for each loan pool is used to calculate historical loss rates that are used as the primary driver of the quantitative historical allowance estimate. The loss emergence and historical loss look-back periods may vary based on a variety of factors. For example, a relatively long look-back may be the appropriate measure during times of economic stability; however, during a period of significant or rapid economic expansion or contraction, a shorter measurement period may be more appropriate. The loss emergence and look back periods may vary by loan pool and are considered in the determination of the historical loss rates for each pool.  </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Management acknowledges that mathematical models have varying levels of inherent limitations and therefore it is always necessary to analyze the model output and apply management judgment.&#160; Accordingly, once the quantitative historical loss rates are established they may be adjusted for qualitative factors to reflect portfolio characteristics, credit concentrations and model imprecision conditions that are not captured in the historical loss rates, recent trends in loan volume and mix, delinquency, local and national economic factors, changes to the Bank&#8217;s lending policies and procedures, experience of lending staff, industrial and geographic factors,  competition and legal or regulatory requirements.  In addition, historical loss rates are modified when loan growth patterns or other trends indicate that the historical loss factors would not accurately reflect losses inherent in the current portfolio.  Final adjustments to the historical loss rate calculation are made for known portfolio characteristics such as 100% cash secured loans and SBA guaranteed loans not captured in the modeling approach.  Simulation techniques such as Monte Carlo modeling, using varying levels of confidence, are used to make such qualitative adjustments.  These simulations help estimate the impact of concentrations such as large loan risk aspects within a loan portfolio and ensure that a reasonable amount of tail risk is captured.  The Monte Carlo output may be adjusted for changes in loss severity based on recent trends that would affect charge-off levels.  All qualitative adjustments are supported with trend (or other relevant data), which are documented in the quarterly allowance for loan loss analysis.  Combining the quantitative and qualitative measurements, the Commercial loan component of our allowance for loan losses is recorded.  </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;">Consumer loan portfolio</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">We estimate the allowance for loan losses for our consumer loan portfolio by estimating the amount of loans that will eventually default based on their current delinquency severity. We then apply a loss rate to the amount of loans that we predict will default based on our historical net loss experience. This amount is then adjusted, as necessary, for qualitative considerations to reflect changes in underwriting, market or industry conditions or based on changes in trends in the composition of the portfolio, including risk composition, seasoning, and underlying collateral. We obtain and review refreshed FICO scores on a quarterly basis, and trends are evaluated for consideration as a qualitative adjustment to the allowance. Other qualitative considerations include, but are not limited to, the evaluation of trends in property values, building permits and unemployment.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;">Impaired loans</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">We consider a commercial loan impaired, when, based on current information, it is probable that we will be unable to collect all amounts of principal and interest due under the original terms of the agreement. Beginning in the second quarter of 2014, we raised the threshold for evaluating commercial loans individually for impairment from $</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;text-decoration:none;">200 thousand</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;to </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$1 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">.  Additionally, all loans (commercial and consumer) modified in a troubled debt restructuring (&#8220;TDR&#8221;), regardless of size, are considered impaired.  The impact of this change to our allowance for loan losses was not significant.  This change was implemented on a prospective basis, accordingly, prior period financial disclosures were not revised.  The need for specific valuation allowances are determined for impaired loans and recorded as necessary.  We measure the impairment in these loans based on the present value of expected future cash flows discounted at the loan&#8217;s effective interest rate or, as a practical alternative, the loan&#8217;s observable market price or the fair value of the underlying collateral, if the loan is collateral dependent.  We then </font></div><br><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:9pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">52</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><br><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">factor any related allowance for loan losses for these loans. Confirmed losses are charged off immediately.  We typically would obtain an appraisal to use as the basis for the fair value of the underlying collateral.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;text-decoration:underline;">Acquired Loans</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;">Acquired loans accounted for under ASC 310-30 (including those accounted for under ASC 310-30 by analogy)</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:6px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">For our acquired loans accounted for under ASC 310-30 for which subsequent decreases to the expected cash flows requires us to evaluate the need for an addition to the allowance for loan losses, our modeling techniques are similar to those we utilize for our originated loans.  To the extent that we experience a deterioration in borrower credit quality resulting in a decrease in our expected cash flows subsequent to the acquisition of the loans, an allowance for loan losses would be established based on our estimate of future credit losses over the remaining life of the loans.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;">Acquired loans accounted for under ASC 310-20</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:6px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">We establish our allowance for loan losses through a provision for credit losses based upon an evaluation process that is similar to our evaluation process used for originated loans. This evaluation, which includes a review of loans on which full collectability may not be reasonably assured, considers, among other matters, the estimated fair value of the underlying collateral, economic conditions, historical net loan loss experience, carrying value of the loans, which includes the remaining net purchase discount or premium, and other factors that warrant recognition in determining our allowance for loan losses.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:bold;">Acquired Loans</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Loans that we acquired in acquisitions subsequent to January&#160;1, 2009 were recorded at fair value with no carryover of the related allowance for loan losses at the time of acquisition. Determining the fair value of the loans involved estimating the amount and timing of principal and interest cash flows expected to be collected on the loans and discounting those cash flows at a market rate of interest.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">We have acquired loans in four separate acquisitions between January 2009 and May 2012. For each acquisition, we reviewed all loans greater than $1&#160;million and considered the following factors as indicators that such an acquired loan had evidence of deterioration in credit quality and was therefore in the scope of Accounting Standards Codification (&#8220;ASC&#8221;) 310-30 (Loans and Debt Securities Acquired with Deteriorated Credit Quality):</font></div><table cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt;"><tr><td style="width:40px;"></td><td></td></tr><tr><td style="vertical-align:top"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;padding-left:16px;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#8226;</font></div></td><td style="vertical-align:top;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Loans that were 90&#160;days or more past due;</font></div></td></tr></table><table cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt;"><tr><td style="width:40px;"></td><td></td></tr><tr><td style="vertical-align:top"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;padding-left:16px;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#8226;</font></div></td><td style="vertical-align:top;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Loans that had an internal risk rating of substandard or worse. Substandard is consistent with regulatory definitions and is defined as having a well defined weakness that jeopardizes liquidation of the loan;</font></div></td></tr></table><table cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt;"><tr><td style="width:40px;"></td><td></td></tr><tr><td style="vertical-align:top"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;padding-left:16px;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#8226;</font></div></td><td style="vertical-align:top;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Loans that were classified as nonaccrual by the acquired bank at the time of acquisition; or</font></div></td></tr></table><table cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt;"><tr><td style="width:40px;"></td><td></td></tr><tr><td style="vertical-align:top"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;padding-left:16px;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#8226;</font></div></td><td style="vertical-align:top;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Loans that had been previously modified in a troubled debt restructuring.</font></div></td></tr></table><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Individual acquired loans determined to have evidence of deterioration in credit quality are accounted for individually in accordance with ASC 310-30.   Any acquired loans that were not individually in the scope of ASC 310-30 because they did not meet the criteria above were either (i)&#160;pooled into groups of similar loans based on the borrower type, loan purpose, and collateral type and accounted for under ASC 310-30 by analogy, or (ii)&#160;accounted for under ASC 310-20 (Nonrefundable Fees and Other Costs).</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Based on the guidance included in the December&#160;18, 2009 letter from the AICPA Depository Institutions Panel to the Office of the Chief Accountant of the SEC, we have made an accounting policy election to apply ASC 310-30 by analogy to qualifying acquired pools of loans that (i)&#160;were acquired in a business combination or asset purchase, (ii)&#160;resulted in recognition of a discount attributable, at least in part, to credit quality, and (iii)&#160;were not subsequently accounted for at fair value.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:18px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;text-decoration:underline;">Acquired loans accounted for under ASC 310-30</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">The excess of expected cash flows from acquired loans over the estimated fair value of acquired loans at acquisition is referred to as the accretable discount and is recognized into interest income over the remaining life </font></div><br><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:9pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">53</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><br><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">of the acquired loans using the interest method. The difference between contractually required payments at acquisition and the cash flows expected to be collected at acquisition is referred to as the nonaccretable discount. The nonaccretable discount represents estimated future credit losses expected to be incurred over the life of the acquired loans. Subsequent decreases to the expected cash flows require us to evaluate the need for an addition to the allowance for loan losses. Subsequent improvements in expected cash flows result in the reversal of a corresponding amount of the nonaccretable discount which we then reclassify as accretable discount that is recognized into interest income over the remaining life of the loan using the interest method. Our evaluation of the amount of future cash flows that we expect to collect takes into account actual credit performance of the acquired loans to date and our best estimates for the expected lifetime credit performance of the loans using currently available information. Charge-offs on acquired loans would be first applied to the nonaccretable discount portion of the fair value adjustment. To the extent that we experience a deterioration in credit quality in our expected cash flows subsequent to the acquisition of the loans, an allowance for loan losses would be established based on our estimate of future credit losses over the remaining life of the loans.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">In accordance with ASC 310-30, recognition of income is dependent on having a reasonable expectation about the timing and amount of cash flows expected to be collected.&#160; We perform such an evaluation on a quarterly basis on both our acquired loans individually accounted for under ASC 310-30 and those in pools accounted for under ASC 310-30 by analogy.&#160; </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Cash flows for acquired loans individually accounted for under ASC 310-30 are estimated on a quarterly basis.&#160; Based on this evaluation, a determination is made as to whether or not we have a reasonable expectation about the timing and amount of cash flows.&#160; Such an expectation includes cash flows from normal customer repayment, foreclosure or other collection efforts.&#160; Cash flows for acquired loans accounted for on a pooled basis under ASC 310-30 by analogy are also estimated on a quarterly basis.&#160; For residential real estate, home equity and other consumer loans, cash flow loss estimates are calculated by a vintage and FICO based model which incorporates a projected forward loss curve.&#160; For commercial loans, lifetime loss rates are assigned to each pool with consideration given for pool make-up, including risk rating profile.&#160; Lifetime loss rates are developed from internally generated loss data and are applied to each pool.&#160; </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">To the extent that we cannot reasonably estimate cash flows, interest income recognition is discontinued.&#160; The unit of account for loans in pools accounted for under ASC 310-30 by analogy is the pool of loans.&#160; Accordingly, as long as we can reasonably estimate cash flows for the pool as a whole, accretable yield on the pool is recognized and all individual loans within the pool - even those more than 90 days past due - would be considered to be accruing interest in our financial statement disclosures, regardless of whether or not we expected to collect any principal or interest cash flows on an individual loan 90 days or more past due.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:bold;">Goodwill</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">We record the excess of the cost of acquired entities over the fair value of identifiable tangible and intangible assets acquired less the fair value of liabilities assumed as goodwill. We do not amortize goodwill and we review it for impairment at our reporting unit level on an annual basis, and when events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts may be impaired.  At </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2013</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, our goodwill totaled </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$1.3 billion</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$2.4 billion</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, respectively.  Of this, approximately </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">95%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">97%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, respectively, was allocated to our Banking reporting unit at </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2013</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">For the quarter ending September 30, 2014, we concluded it was more likely than not that the fair value of our Banking reporting unit was less than its carrying value including goodwill, given our current expectations regarding the macroeconomic and industry environment, including our view of future interest rates and our current stock price range.  Accordingly, we performed a &#8220;Step 1&#8221; review for possible goodwill impairment in advance of our annual impairment testing date. Determining the fair value of the Banking reporting unit as part of the Step 1 analysis involves significant judgment. For Step 1, we used a market approach to determine the fair value.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">In our application of the market approach for our Banking reporting unit, we utilized a 35% control premium assumption based on our review of transactions observable in the market place that we determined were </font></div><br><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:9pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">54</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><br><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">comparable plus the fair value of our outstanding preferred stock and applied market based multiples to the tangible book value and projected earnings of our Banking reporting unit.  The projected earnings multiple used was 10x and was based on a stock price for assessment purposes of </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$7.37</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;per share and was applied to our projected 2014 and 2015 earnings.  The tangible book value multiple used was 1.14x and was based on a </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$7.37</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;stock price and tangible book value at the assessment date.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Based on our review, we concluded that the carrying amount of the Banking reporting unit exceeded its estimated fair value and thus performed &#8220;Step 2.&#8221;  For Step 2, we compared the implied fair value of the Banking reporting unit's goodwill with the carrying amount of the goodwill for the Banking reporting unit.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">The implied fair value of goodwill is determined in the same manner as goodwill that is recognized in a business combination. Significant judgment and estimates are involved in the determination of the fair value of the assets and liabilities of the reporting units, and therefore directly impact the implied fair value of goodwill, as part of this Step 2 analysis. The most significant estimates involved related to our Banking reporting unit are the fair valuation of our loans and core deposit intangible asset. We determined the fair value of our loan portfolio by utilizing a methodology wherein similar loans were aggregated into pools.  Cash flows for each pool were determined by estimating future credit losses and the rate of prepayments.  Projected cash flows were then discounted to present value based on a market rate for similar loans. We estimated the value of the core deposit intangible asset using a discounted cash flow approach considering market comparable transactions. Both of these estimates are highly subjective and involve many judgments.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Based on our assessments under both Steps 1 and 2, we recorded an impairment of our Banking reporting unit goodwill of </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$1.1 billion</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;as of September 30, 2014.  Upon our annual goodwill analysis, we concluded that no additional impairment was necessary.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">For our annual impairment test of our Banking reporting unit as of November 1, 2014, we used a market approach to determine the fair value in Step 1 of the analysis.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">In our application of the market approach for our Banking reporting unit, we utilized a 35% control premium assumption based on our review of transactions observable in the market place that we determined were comparable plus the fair value of our outstanding preferred stock and applied market based multiples to the tangible book value and projected earnings of our Banking reporting unit.  The projected earnings multiples used were 10.5x and 12.1x and were based on a stock price for assessment purposes of $7.49 per share and was applied to our projected 2014 and 2015 earnings, respectively.  The tangible book value multiple used was 1.1x and was based on a $7.49 stock price and tangible book value at the assessment date.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Based on our review, we concluded that the carrying amount of the Banking reporting unit exceeded its estimated fair value and thus performed &#8220;Step 2.&#8221;  For Step 2, we compared the implied fair value of the Banking reporting unit's goodwill with the carrying amount of the goodwill for the Banking reporting unit.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">The most significant estimates involved related to our November 1, 2014 assessment of our Banking reporting unit were made in a similar manner as our September 30, 2014 assessment.  Based on our assessments under both Steps 1 and 2, no further impairment was warranted. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Negative changes to the assumptions necessary for the determination of the significant estimates used in computing fair value of our Banking reporting unit would result in further impairment.  A 5% reduction to the price of our common stock utilized in the impairment test would result in a further write down of the fair value of our Banking reporting unit by approximately $175 million.  A five percentage point decline in the control premium assumption to 30% changes the overall fair value of our Banking reporting unit by approximately $130 million. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">For our Financial Services reporting unit, we perform our annual impairment review of goodwill on November 1 of each year utilizing valuation methods we believe appropriate, given the availability and applicability of market based inputs for those methods.  After giving appropriate consideration to all available information at that point in time, we determined that the fair value of the Financial Services reporting unit exceeded its carrying value (Step 1) and, therefore, there was no impairment of goodwill in 2014.  For Step 1, we used both an income approach and a </font></div><br><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:9pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">55</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><br><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">market approach to determine the fair value.  Our income approach was based upon assumptions of income statement activity. An internal forecast was developed through consideration of current year financial performance and near term expectations regarding key business drivers. Long-term growth rates of 3% were then applied in determining the terminal value. A discount rate of 14% was used based upon consideration of the risk free rate, leverage factors, equity risk premium, and Company specific risk factors. In our market approach for our financial services reporting unit, we utilized a 35% control premium assumption based on our review of transactions observable in the market place that we determined were comparable to earnings for our financial services reporting unit. The market and income approaches were weighted equally.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">At December 31, 2014, we concluded it was not more likely than not that the fair value of our Banking and Financial Services reporting units were less than their carrying values including goodwill.  Consideration was given to our current expectations regarding the macroeconomic and industry environment, including our view of future interest rates and our current stock price range.  Accordingly, we were not required to perform a Step 1 analysis as of December 31, 2014. </font></div><a name="s7B0C9B2025155827856609E17F08972D"></a><div These increases were partially offset by a </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$196 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, or </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">5%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">decrease</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;in residential real estate loans and a </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$25 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, or </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">8%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">decrease</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;in other consumer loans.  </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">The yield on our commercial real estate and commercial business loan portfolios decreased by </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">41</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;basis points and </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">15</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;basis points, respectively, as a result of repayments and reinvestments at current market rates.  Consumer loan yields dropped </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">27</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;basis points during the same period, driven primarily by a </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">26</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;basis points decline in indirect auto yields, </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">13</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;basis points decline in residential real estate, and </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">18</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;basis points decline in home equity yields.  Partially offsetting these declines was a </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">30</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;basis points </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">increase</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;in credit card yields and </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">12</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;basis points </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">increase</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;in other consumer loan yields.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-left:4px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Commercial loan yields&#160;declined as a result&#160;of (i) new loan production being booked in a lower interest rate environment, and (ii) a shorter duration of our commercial loan portfolio.&#160; The shorter duration resulted as a higher percentage of our new originations were variable rate, which was&#160;partially attributable to our customer derivatives capacity, which&#160;permits us to offer our customers seeking a longer term rate the flexibility to swap their variable loan obligation to a fixed rate.  These variable rate originations replaced the repayment of fixed rate loans with higher rates primarily in the commercial real estate portfolio.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-left:4px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">During </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, our average interest-bearing deposits </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">decreased</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$138 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, or less than </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">1%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, and rates paid were unchanged from 2013, while average short-term borrowings </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">increased</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$934 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, or </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">25%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, as a result of our decision to fund our balance sheet growth and rotation through low cost short-term borrowings.  This funding strategy has also </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">decreased</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;the rate paid on borrowings by </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">15</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;basis points.  Noninterest-bearing deposits, which </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">increased</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$461 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, or </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">10%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, also served as a funding source during </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-left:4px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;font-style:normal;font-weight:bold;text-transform:default;">2013</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:bold;">&#32;compared to </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;font-style:normal;font-weight:bold;text-transform:default;">2012</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:bold;">&#32;</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Our net interest income increased 6.9% to $1.1 billion in 2013 from $1.0 billion in 2012. The year over year increase primarily reflected our $1.6 billion increase in average interest earning assets to $32.8 billion, which was largely attributable to the full year impact of the HSBC Branch Acquisition and continued organic growth in our commercial and indirect auto loan portfolios offset in large part due to lower asset yields.  The increase in average interest earning assets outpaced the growth in average interest bearing liabilities, which increased $1.0 billion year over year, resulting in a $518 million increase in net earning assets to $5.9 billion in 2013. The increase, on a taxable equivalent basis, in net interest income due to the increase in our average net earning assets was approximately $102 million.  In addition, our net interest income benefited from approximately $19&#160;million in accretable yield attributable to better than expected credit performance of certain acquired loans.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-left:4px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Our average balance of investment securities decreased year over year by approximately $752 million as we executed our balance sheet rotation strategy of using repayments on our securities portfolio to fund loan growth. The decrease in average balance was offset by an increase in yield of 18 basis points during 2013.  The increase in yield was primarily due to lower premium amortization on residential mortgage-backed securities in the current year partially offset by reinvestment in lower yielding assets.  </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">As of December 31, 2013, the amount of net premiums on our residential mortgage-backed securities to be recognized in future periods amounted to approximately $71 million, which equates to a weighted average premium above par of approximately 1.3%. Subsequent changes to the interest rate environment will continue to impact our yield earned on these securities.  Cash flows from collateralized mortgage obligations ("CMOs") in the current year were almost $600 million lower than the approximately $1.9 billion in cash flows expected at the beginning of the year.  Such slower prepayments delay and elongate the period over which the premium is amortized.  Also contributing to the increase in yields was the prepayment of CLOs that were purchased at a </font></div><br><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:9pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">57</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><br><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">discount.  During 2013, we recognized $3 million of interest income related to these prepayments.  While such income from CLO payoffs benefit the quarter in which they are recognized, the long-term implication is that these assets had above market interest rates that are being replaced with other lower yielding assets.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-left:4px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Overall, average loans increased 13%, or $2.4 billion, in 2013.  Commercial loans increased 14%, or $1.6 billion, as our pipeline remained strong throughout the year.  Indirect auto contributed approximately one-third of the average net loan growth in 2013.  Our average indirect auto portfolio increased $849 million, as we originated $1.3 billion in new loans during 2013.  These increases were partially offset by a slight decrease in our residential real estate loans.  Loan yields declined 36 basis points as commercial loan yields decreased by 46 basis points and our total consumer loan portfolio yields decreased by 17 basis points.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-left:4px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Our average balances of interest bearing deposits increased by $2.0 billion reflecting the full year impact of the HSBC Branch Acquisition offset by current year declines in money market deposits and certificates of deposit.  Our average rate paid declined by nine basis points due to our previous deposit pricing actions and competitive rate pressure.  Demand for longer term certificates of deposit remains weak.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-left:4px;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Our average borrowings decreased year over year by approximately $1.0 billion as a result of paying down borrowings upon closing of the HSBC Branch Acquisition, partially offset by our decision to fund our balance sheet growth and rotation through low cost short-term borrowings.  This funding strategy also decreased the rate paid on borrowings by 16 basis points.</font></div><br><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:9pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">58</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><br><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">The following table presents our condensed average balance sheet and taxable equivalent interest income and yields.  Yields earned on interest-earning assets, rates paid on interest-bearing liabilities and average balances are based on average daily balances:</font></div><div name="s25D64D25578657888BB0EC66646C4906"></a><br><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:bold;">PROVISION FOR CREDIT LOSSES</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:6px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Our provision for credit losses is comprised of three components: consideration of the adequacy of our allowance for originated loan losses; needs for allowance for acquired loan losses due to deterioration in credit quality subsequent to acquisition; and probable losses associated with our unfunded loan commitments.  </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">On February 24, 2015, the Company announced that its management had preliminarily determined that the Company&#8217;s allowance for loan losses (&#8220;allowance&#8221;) for the period ending December 31, 2014 and disclosed in the Company&#8217;s press release filed on Form 8-K on January 23, 2015 was overstated due to the misconduct of a mid-level employee.  </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Management and the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors have conducted investigations into this matter. The Audit Committee&#8217;s investigation found no evidence that others within the Company were aware of or participated in the employee misconduct, including senior and executive management.  We have also concluded that there was no material error in our previously issued financial statements.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Our review of the allowance for each quarter back to the second quarter 2013 included both qualitative and quantitative components, which include both modeled and judgmental factors.  Overall, the quarterly adjustments were immaterial and range from $1 to $5 million variance to our previously reported provision for loan losses.  The cumulative impact reduced our allowances as of December 31, 2014 by $7 million to </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$234 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;resulting in a ratio of originated allowance to originated loans of </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">1.18%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">.  While these adjustments did change the amount of our estimated allowance, the adjustments do not represent cash losses and our reported net charge-offs have not changed.  Further, our review revealed no new, negative information regarding the high credit quality of our portfolio.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">The information in this Annual Report on Form 10-K, including our consolidated financial statements, reflects the allowance adjustments we have made as described above.  For further information, see Item 6, &#8220;Selected Financial Data.&#8221;</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Additionally, we have concluded that internal controls over the process to determine the allowance were insufficient to prevent a potential error from being material.  Importantly, we are making changes to our internal controls over the determination of the allowance as part of our remediation plan.  See &#8220;Managements Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting&#8221;, in Item 8 &#8220;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data.&#8221;</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">The following table details the composition of our provision for credit losses for the periods The provision for credit losses related to originated loans amounted to </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$85 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, or </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">0.47%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;of average originated loans, for </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, compared to </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$96 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, or </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">0.64%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;of average originated loans, for </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2013</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">.  The provision for </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;covered net charge-offs of </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$62 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, and included $5 million to cover exposure to borrowers servicing the energy sector following the recent fall in oil prices, and $5 million related to impairment of a commercial loan that </font></div><br><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:9pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">61</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><a name="s25D64D25578657888BB0EC66646C4906"></a><br><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:12px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">was sold in March 2015.  The provision for </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2013</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;included </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$44 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;to support sequential originated loan growth and </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$52 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;to cover net charge offs.  </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">We recorded an additional $5 million of provision expense in the fourth quarter of 2014 to cover exposure to borrowers servicing the energy sector following the recent fall in oil prices.  Our direct exposure to the oil and gas industry is about </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$141 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;in balances, or </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">0.6%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;of our total loan portfolio.  Additionally, our indirect exposure to the sector is about </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$144 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;in balances, or </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">0.6%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;of our total loan portfolio. After we issued our fourth quarter 2014 earnings release on January 23, 2015 but prior to filing our Form 10-K, we obtained new information that increased our fourth quarter net charge-offs and provision for credit losses by $10 million and $16 million, respectively. These increases reflect 1) $11 million provision expense to cover a $10 million charge-off and $1 million of additional reserve related to a single borrower in the oil and gas industry for which we obtained new information regarding the collectability of the customer loan (See &#8220;Energy Related Exposures&#8221; in &#8220;Credit Risk&#8221; for our portfolio details) and 2) a $5 million provision for credit losses related to impairment on a commercial loan that was sold in March 2015. Our net charge-offs for the first quarter of 2015 will reflect the $5 million loss related to the sale of this commercial loan.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Our provision for loan losses related to our acquired loans is based upon a deterioration in expected cash flows subsequent to the acquisition of the loans.  These acquired loans were originally recorded at fair value on the date of acquisition. As the fair value at time of acquisition incorporated lifetime expected credit losses, there was no carryover of the related allowance for loan losses.  Subsequent to acquisition, we periodically reforecast the expected cash flows for our acquired loans and compare this to our original estimates to evaluate the need for a loan loss provision. Our provision related to our acquired loans was </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$8 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;for </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$7 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;for </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2013</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">. style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;color:#000000;text-decoration:none;">decreased</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;</font><font capital markets and bank owned life insurance income.  Partially offsetting these decreases were higher merchant and card fees and revenues from wealth management services.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">A portion of the decrease in deposit service charges, approximately $5 million, was related to the process issue while this revenue source continues to be pressured by lower customer incident rates consistent with industry trends.  The </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">18%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;decrease in capital markets income was driven by lower derivative fee income partially offset by modestly higher syndication fees.  Long-term fixed rate pricing and competitive terms in the market place, coupled with the impact of the Dodd-Frank Act, has resulted in diminished customer demand for interest rate derivatives.  The </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$5 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;decrease in other income was primarily due to lower investment income.  During 2014, we recorded </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$33 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;in amortization for certain historic tax credit investments.  These investments are amortized in the first year of funding and we recognized the amortization as contra-fee income, included in other income, with an offsetting benefit that reduced our income tax expense. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Merchant and card fees </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">increased</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">3%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;during the </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">year ended December 31, 2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;from the same period in </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2013</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, stemming from higher debit card revenues and volume driven interchange fees.  Wealth management services income </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">increased</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">$3 million</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, or </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">5%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">, for the </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">year ended December 31, 2014</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;from the same period in </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">2013</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;driven by growth in annuity sales resulting from favorable spreads between time deposits and fixed annuity rates.  Bank owned life insurance income </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">decreased</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">10%</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">&#32;from elevated 2013 levels.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">2013</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">&#32;compared to </font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">2012</font><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">&#32;</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Noninterest income increased $6 million for 2013 compared to 2012.  Noninterest income for 2012 included a $21 million gain on securities portfolio repositioning.  Excluding this gain, the increase from 2012 to 2013 was $27 million and resulted primarily from the full year impact of our May 2012 HSBC Branch Acquisition.  Deposit service charges also benefited from higher collection rates.  The acquisition of the credit card business in our HSBC Branch </font></div><br><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;font-size:9pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:9pt;">63</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><a name="s4DF8F62C72565627A6330D2C3E0405EF"></a><br><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">Acquisition and continued expansion of this business both contributed to the $10 million, or 26%, increase in merchant and card fees.  The acquisition of $2.5 billion in assets under management from HSBC and subsequent growth in assets under management contributed to the $17 million, or 41%, increase in revenues from wealth management services.  Additionally, as annuity issuers widened spreads on fixed annuities relative to certificates of deposit rates during 2013, fixed annuities became a popular product for our customers.  These increases were partially offset by a $14 million, or 42%, decrease in mortgage banking revenues and a $4 million, or 17%, decrease in capital markets revenues.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">The decrease in mortgage banking revenues in 2013 from 2012 were due to rising mortgage rates in the second half of 2013, which negatively impacted application volumes and gain on sale margins.&#160; Sold originations to the secondary market were relatively flat from 2012 levels as rising rates (which drove lower originations) was muted as 2013 reflected a full year of HSBC loan production employees and the branch network.&#160; Gain on sale margins were compressed due to increased competition, guaranty fee increases and spread tightening between the primary (rates to borrowers) and secondary (mortgage backed securities) rates.&#160; The gain on sale reductions were slightly offset by higher servicing income driven by higher net service fees on a growing serviced-for-others portfolio.&#160; With increasing rates and lower refinance volumes, our focus going forward will be on the purchase market to enable market share growth.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;">The decrease in capital markets revenues was primarily due to increased competition and the impact of Dodd-Frank Act's definition of Eligible Market Participants for derivative and swap transactions.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:bold;">NONINTEREST EXPENSES</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:left;font-size:11pt;"><font
